newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - German village try to revive Bismarck's birthplace.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - German village try to revive Bismarck's birthplace.

text.p: Residents of this decaying east German village still remember nearly 40 years ago when Schoenhausen Castle, the birthplace of Otto von Bismarck, the man who first united Germany, was razed to the ground.
Remembering the moment the castle went up in smoke, Brigitte Neumann said: "The military sealed off the castle for a week and carried out manoeuvres.
"One afternoon we all heard explosions and saw a huge dust cloud rise above it," said Neumann, a retired nurse. "No one said anything openly, but there was silent outrage."
East Germany's Communists were trying to stamp out all trace of the "Iron Chancellor" from the place where his family were lords of the manor for more than 400 years.

Six years after Germany reunited, Bismarck's fame as the man who first brought the country together in 1871 and served as its chancellor for 19 years, is virtually the only hope of survival for one of the country's poorest communities.

The village, 150 km (90 miles) west of Berlin, wants to promote itself as Bismarck's birthplace, but residents regret they will never be able to bring back the castle, built in 1700, where only the left wing was left standing.
An east German family were housed in the near ruins. Today it looks partially destroyed, with a ragged edge of bricks along the outer wall that once adjoined the castle.
COMMUNIST CAMPAIGN TO WIPE OUT THE PAST

Historians say the castle, part of the family's 400 hectare (988 acres) estate, was razed on August 2, 1958 -- the same day as Puttbus Castle on an island in the Baltic sea and Berlin's royal palace, the residence of Germany's last kaiser, Wilhelm II, were destroyed.

"In communist times it counted as a slur to be from Schoenhausen," said Neumann, 56, who remembers how, as a 10-year-old, she was punished at school after revealing that her grandmother worked in the Bismarcks' kitchen in the days of the kaiser.
"I couldn't understand what I'd said wrong," said Neumann, who was ordered to stand in a corner for an hour.
"It was taboo to talk about the old days."

Neumann's early experience spurred a lifelong quest to gather as much local information as possible about Bismarck and his family in the region. Today she gives guided tours of the district and its historical landmarks.

"I had a friend in charge of the old paper collection who let me comb through it from the early 1960s," said Neumann, whose findings include pre-World War One postcards with "greetings from Bismarck's birthplace" and old newspapers.
"People were afraid to keep these things so whenever they cleared out their homes they threw them away," she said.
In East Germany there was little information about the man who Bismarck brought dozens of disparate German principalities and lands together for the first time.
The official line was that he was a leading member of the ruling class who exploited the workers.
BISMARCK'S FAME KEY TO VILLAGE REVIVAL

Communist ideology, which permeated peoples' lives even if they did not believe in it, makes it hard for Schoenhausen's largely agricultural community to market itself and its historical assets successfully.
One setback is that Bismarck's birthplace appears not to be in a single German or foreign travel guide. But history fans have tracked down the landmark on their own initiative.

"We had the idea of marketing Schoenhausen as Bismarck's birthplace because so many visitors from Germany, as well as America and Japan, starting arriving and asking us where he was born," said Norbert Tanne, the mayor of Schoenhausen.
"We hope to boost our community by making this a thriving tourist attraction and creating more jobs," he said.

Schoenhausen's population dropped from about 4,000 to 2,300 after unification in 1990, in a region where unemployment currently runs at 23 percent -- one of Germany's highest rates -- as the young left to find work elsewhere.

The plan is to renovate the remaining wing of the castle -- the family that lived there moved out 18 months ago -- and convert it into a Bismarck museum. At present it serves as a makeshift tourist information office.

In his lifetime, Bismarck had opened a museum in Schoenhausen devoted to himself to display portraits, busts and presents from across the world including ethnic jewellery, tribal artifacts from Africa and beer tankards.
The castle wing is surrounded by a public park, which Tanne plans to have restored to its former glory, with reconstructed entrance gates and paths lined with original sandstone statues.

He also wants to bring back many of the former museum's exhibits. Bismarck's family transferred some in 1927 to another private museum in Friedrichsruh, near Hamburg, where they still live on one of the old Bismarck estates.
But many presents were dispersed across former East Germany in the communist era and some are feared lost forever.
"Our main problem is financial. We need 1.5 million marks ($950,000) to restore the wing and set up the museum and we just don't have that kind of money," said Tanne.
"But we are hoping to get something from the regional authorities, from central government or private sponsors."
Tanne hopes the new museum will be ready for 1998 when he plans a grand opening to mark the 100th anniversary of Bismarck's death.
"We have had about 6,000 visitors in both 1995 and 1996. We have a few hotels and guest houses, as well as farm houses where visitors could stay," he said.

A dozen members of the Bismarck clan met in Schoenhausen in 1995 for their first reunion there since the end of World War Two, when Otto von Bismarck's direct descendants fled what was then the Soviet zone of occupation.
Bismarck is buried in Friedrichsruh.
